metadata.title: New and Revised Draft Q&As on Biosimilar Development and the BPCI Act (Revision 4): Draft Guidance for Industry

The use of 61 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 62 not required. 63

candidates.statement: A BLA submitted under section 351(k) (known as a 351(k) BLA ) of the PHS Act must contain, 83 among other things, information demonstrating that the biological product is biosimilar to a 84 reference product based upon data derived from analytical studies, an assessment of toxicity, and 85 a clinical study or studies (see section 351(k)(2)(A)(i)(I) of the PHS Act), unless FDA has 86 determined that an element described in section 351(k)(2)(A)(i)(I) is unnecessary (see section 87 351(k)(2)(A)(ii) of the PHS Act). To meet the standard for interchangeability , an applicant must 88 provide sufficient information to demonstrate biosimilarity to the reference product and also to 89 demonstrate that the biological product can be expected to produce the same clinical result as the 90 reference product in any given patient, and if the biological product is administered more than 91 once to an individual, the risk in terms of safety or diminished efficacy of alternating or 92 switching between the use of the biological product and the reference product is not greater than 93 the risk of using the reference product without such alternation or switch (see section 351(k)(4) 94 of the PHS Act). Interchangeable products may be substituted for the reference product without 95 the intervention of the prescribing health care provider (see section 351(i)(3) of the PHS Act). 96
candidates.context: Section 351(i) of the PHS Act defines biosimilarity to mean “that the biological product is highly 77 similar to the reference product notwithstanding minor differences in clinically inactive 78 components” and that “there are no clinically meaningful differences between the biological 79 product and the reference product in terms of the safety, purity, and potency of the product” (see 80 section 351(i)(2) of the PHS Act). 81 “Question-and-Answer” Guidance Format 98

candidates.statement: For purposes of the comparative analytical assessment and comparison between 210 the non-U.S.-licensed comparator product and the U.S.-licensed reference 211 product, any lots used in a clinical study supporting a demonstration of 212 biosimilarity should be included in the comparative analytical assessment 213 intended to justify the relevance of comparative data with the non-U.S.-licensed 214 comparator product to a demonstration of biosimilarity. 8 Specifically, if a clinical 215 study compares the proposed biosimilar to a non-U.S.-licensed comparator 216 product, sponsors should ensure that data generated in that clinical study are 217 relevant and applicable to the demonstration of biosimilarity by providing 218 sufficient comparative analytical data based on: (1) the lots of the non-U.S.- 219 licensed comparator product used in the clinical study; and (2) the lots of the 220 U.S.-licensed reference product used in the comparative analytical assessment to 221 support a demonstration that the proposed biosimilar is highly similar to the U.S.- 222 licensed reference product. If analytical differences are observed between the 223 clinical lots of the non-U.S.-licensed comparator product and the U.S.-licensed 224 reference product lots used in the comparative analytical assessment with the 225 proposed biosimilar, the sponsor may provide information (e.g., a risk assessment 226 and relevant analytical data) to scientifically justify why these differences do not 227 preclude a conclusion that the data from the clinical study comparing the 228 proposed biosimilar to the non-U.S.-licensed comparator product are relevant to 229 the demonstration of biosimilarity. 230
candidates.context: A.I.8.b Reference Product and Non-U.S.-Licensed Comparator Products 7 The acceptance criteria used to support a demonstration that a proposed biosimilar 232 product is highly similar to the U.S.-licensed reference product should be derived 233 from data generated from a sponsor’s analysis of the U.S.-licensed reference 234 product. The comparative analytical assessment should be based on a direct 235 comparison of the proposed biosimilar product to the U.S.-licensed reference 236 product. As a scientific matter, combining data from the U.S.-licensed reference 237 product and non-U.S.-licensed comparator product to determine the acceptance 238 criteria or to perform the comparative analytical assessment for the proposed 239 product would not be acceptable to support a demonstration that the proposed 240 product is biosimilar to the U.S.-licensed reference product. 241

candidates.statement: Q.I.10. How long and in what manner should sponsors retain reserve samples of the 252 biological products used in comparative clinical PK and/or PD studies intended 253 to support a 351(k) application? 254 [Revised in Draft March 2026] 255
candidates.context: A.I.10. Reserve samples establish the identity of the products tested in the actual study, 257 allow for confirmation of the validity and reliability of the results of the study, 258 and facilitate investigation of further follow-up questions that arise after the 259 studies are completed. FDA recommends that the sponsor of a proposed 260 biosimilar product retain reserve samples for at least 5 years following the date on 261 which the 351(k) application is licensed, or, if such application is not licensed, at 262 least 5 years following the date of completion of a comparative clinical 263 pharmacokinetic (PK) and/or pharmacodynamic (PD) study of the reference 264 product and the proposed biosimilar product (or other clinical study in which PK 265 or PD samples are collected with the primary objective of assessing PK or PD 266 similarity) that is intended to support a submission under se

candidates.statement: A.I.12. Under section 351(k)(2)(A)(i)(IV) of the PHS Act, an applicant must 298 demonstrate that the “strength” of the proposed biosimilar product or proposed 299 interchangeable product is the same as that of the reference product. Data and 300 information generated as part of the analytical similarity assessment may inform 301 the determination that a proposed biosimilar product or proposed interchangeable 302 product has the same strength as its reference product. As a scientific matter, there 303 may be a need to take into account different factors and approaches in 304 determining the strength of different biological products. Sponsors should discuss 305 their proposed approach with FDA and provide an adequate scientific basis for 306 their approach to demonstrating same strength. 307

candidates.statement: A.I.19. A sponsor may submit a single investigational new drug application (IND) for a 342 development program that is intended to support licensure of a proposed product 343 under section 351(k) of the PHS Act and includes use of a non-U.S.-licensed 344 comparator product. The sponsor should submit information supporting the 345 proposed clinical investigation with the non-U.S.-licensed comparator product 346 under the IND. This scenario may occur if a sponsor seeks to use data from a 347 clinical study comparing its proposed biosimilar product to a non-U.S.-licensed 348 comparator product to address, in part, the requirements under section 349 351(k)(2)(A) of the PHS Act. For example, a sponsor may propose to conduct a 350 clinical PK study in the United States with the proposed biosimilar product and a 351 non-U.S.-licensed comparator product. 352
candidates.context: Q.I.19. If a non-U.S.-licensed comparator product is proposed for importation and use 336 in the United States in a clinical investigation intended to support licensure of a 337 proposed product under section 351(k), is a separate IND required for the non- 338 U.S.-licensed product? 339 [Revised in Draft March 2026 ] 340 A non-U.S.-licensed comparator product is considered an investigational new drug 354 in the United States, and thus would require an IND for importation and use in the 355 United States (see 21 CFR 312.110(a)). If a sponsor intends to conduct a clinical 356 investigation in the United States using a non-U.S.-licensed comparator product, 357 the IND requirements in 21 CFR part 312 also would apply to this product (see, 358 e.g., 21 CFR 312.2). 359

This should include, to the greatest extent possible, summary approval 386 information and current product labeling made public by the foreign regulatory 387 authority. In addition, a sponsor should also provide information on the 388 conditions and containers that will be used to transport the drug product to the 389 U.S. clinical site(s) and information on the relabeling and repackaging operations 390 that will be used to relabel the drug product for investigational use. This should 391 include information on how exposure of the product to light and temperature 392 conditions outside of the recommended storage conditions will be prevented. A 393 risk assessment on the impact the relabeling operations may have on drug product 394 stability should also be included. 395
